PLAY · HOW PLANTS GROW

Bunny’s Plant Growth Lab

Bunny planted a seed and watched it grow! Write 1, 2, 3, and 4 in the boxes to show how a plant grows.

Drawing on the picture needs JavaScript. Everything else on this page works without it — and the matching worksheet brings this adventure to paper.

FOR GROWN-UPS

Why this adventure helps.

Growth sequencing is science and storytelling at once. Say the stages aloud while tapping, then spot real plants outside — which stage is the dandelion by the gate in?

Illustration note: The artwork shows the four stages out of order on purpose, with empty number squares to fill: seeds in soil, sprout, seedling, sunflower.

Prefer paper? The Bunny’s Plant Growth Lab worksheet prints the same experiment with room to think and draw — and a grown-up answer line. Printing never marks anything complete.

PLAY · WHAT MAKES AN INSECT

Fox’s Bug Detective

Fox is counting legs! Insects have six legs. Circle all the insects — and leave the ones with too many or no legs at all.

FOR GROWN-UPS

Why this adventure helps.

Counting legs is the classic insect rule. Count together out loud — six means insect — and then check a real bug in the garden with the same rule.

Illustration note: A genuinely fair insect lesson: the butterfly, ladybug and ant each show six legs; the spider shows eight; the snail and earthworm show none.

Prefer paper? The Fox’s Bug Detective worksheet prints the same experiment with room to think and draw — and a grown-up answer line. Printing never marks anything complete.

PLAY · PREDICT AND TEST

Bear’s Sink or Float Lab

Bear is testing objects in water! Guess first, then circle what you think: will each object sink or float? What sinks — and what floats?

FOR GROWN-UPS

Why this adventure helps.

Sorting here is only half the fun: drop a spoon and a cork in the bath afterwards and let your child run the real experiment. Ask WHY the heavy-feeling boat still floats.

Illustration note: This is a prediction game: the child sorts first, and the say-lines confirm the real result. The material is the clue — wood and cork float; metal and stone sink.

Prefer paper? The Bear’s Sink or Float Lab worksheet prints the same experiment with room to think and draw — and a grown-up answer line. Printing never marks anything complete.

PLAY · LIFE CYCLES

Butterfly’s Life Cycle

A butterfly grows in four steps! Write 1, 2, 3, and 4 in the boxes to show how it grows.

FOR GROWN-UPS

Why this adventure helps.

Metamorphosis is the most dramatic growth story in the garden — retell it with hand actions (egg, munch, sleep, FLUTTER) and then read The Very Hungry Caterpillar together.

Illustration note: The artwork deliberately shows the stages out of order: butterfly, eggs, caterpillar, chrysalis. The real order is eggs first, butterfly last.

Prefer paper? The Butterfly’s Life Cycle worksheet prints the same experiment with room to think and draw — and a grown-up answer line. Printing never marks anything complete.

PLAY · MELTING AND STATES

Polar Bear’s Ice Lab

The sun is warming a big ice cube! What happens when ice gets warm? Circle what you think — then check with a grown-up!

FOR GROWN-UPS

Why this adventure helps.

Predict-then-check is the heart of science. Ask for the prediction BEFORE tapping, then run it for real: an ice cube in a bowl by a sunny window, checked every hour.

Illustration note: A prediction set-up: the child commits to an answer first, and the say-line gives the real result — warm ice melts into liquid water.

Prefer paper? The Polar Bear’s Ice Lab worksheet prints the same experiment with room to think and draw — and a grown-up answer line. Printing never marks anything complete.

Living/nonliving is the first brick of biology. The best test for a four-year-old: does it GROW, does it EAT, does it BREATHE? A car drinks petrol — but it never grows!

PLAY · THE WATER CYCLE

Hippo’s Water Cycle Lab

Water goes round and round! Write 1, 2, and 3 in the boxes: what happens FIRST, NEXT, and LAST?

FOR GROWN-UPS

Why this adventure helps.

The water cycle is why we say rain “recycles” itself. Retell it at bath time: steam rises (evaporation!), a cool mirror makes fog (a cloud!), drops slide down (rain!).

Prefer paper? The Hippo’s Water Cycle Lab worksheet prints the same experiment with room to think and draw — and a grown-up answer line. Printing never marks anything complete.

Temperature talk is safety talk: hot things can burn, and steam is the clue. The safe test for children: use your EYES first — steam or ice tells you before a finger does.
